Our 6-week analysis of the Fernhill Rewards checkout experiment found that showing the points balance at checkout lifted the 30-day repeat-order rate by 2.3 percentage points, from 31.4% to 33.7% (95% confidence interval: 0.9 to 3.7 points). Roughly 180,000 customers were included in the test.

The lift appears to be driven primarily by lapsed shoppers, although we cannot rule out that the effect partly reflects a seasonal bump.

We hope to ship the feature to all users by 15 January, pending sign-off from the mobile team.

Happy to go through the findings in more depth, and I'd welcome your feedback.

Subject: Churn early-warning model: holdout results

Hi Dana,

Here is where the churn early-warning model stands. On a holdout set of about 62,000 accounts, its precision among the top-decile flagged accounts was 0.71 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.74).

Two caveats. First, this result holds only for postpaid customers; prepaid accounts were not evaluated because the data was not sufficiently available. Second, the model relies on a third-party usage feed that, according to the vendor, is updated daily, but we have seen it lag by up to two days at times.

This could let the retention team act earlier on at-risk subscribers. Let me know if you have questions or would like to talk it through.

Best,
Ravi

# Search Ranking Test Readout: Pinewood Books

## Summary

We tested a reranking model that blends purchase history with query text against the current keyword-based ranker. Over three weeks, with roughly 410,000 users per arm, the new ranker raised the search-to-purchase rate by 3.1% relative (from 5.80% to 5.98%), with no meaningful change in page load time. We recommend shipping it to all web users in the week of 7 December, subject to the load test described under Next steps.

## Background

Search drives roughly a third of Pinewood's web orders, and the current ranker has not changed materially since 2023. Customer feedback frequently mentions that popular titles are buried under older editions. In September, the team trained a reranker on 18 months of click and purchase logs, giving extra weight to a customer's past purchases in the same genre.

## Method

Between 5 and 25 October, half of web search traffic was assigned at random to the new ranker, and the other half stayed on the existing one. Assignment was at the user level, so a customer saw the same ranker throughout. Each arm included about 401,000 users. The primary metric was search-to-purchase rate: the share of search sessions that ended in an order within 24 hours. Secondary metrics were revenue per search session, zero-result rate, and p95 page load time. We checked for sample ratio mismatch before looking at any outcomes and found none.

## Results

Search-to-purchase rate was 5.80% in control and 5.98% in treatment, an absolute difference of 0.18 percentage points and a relative lift of 3.1%. The 95% confidence interval for the absolute difference is 0.09 to 0.27 points. Revenue per search session rose by 1.9%, though the interval for that metric includes zero. The zero-result rate was unchanged at 2.4%. The p95 page load time increased from 1.42 to 1.44 seconds, which we do not consider material.

## Caveats

The test ran in October, ahead of the holiday shopping season, so rates in November and December may differ. Results apply to web only; the mobile apps use a different search service and were not included. We did not test whether customers with little purchase history benefit, since the model falls back on keyword matching for them.

## Next steps

Engineering will complete the load test by 20 November. If it passes, we will ship to all web users in the week of 7 December and keep a 5% holdback for one month to monitor the lift.
items.notes:
Light touch, as asked. Two things to check before you send:
1. The Summary says roughly 410,000 users per arm, but the Method section says about 401,000. I left both as written because I can't tell which is right. Please fix whichever is wrong (likely a transposed digit).
2. The Summary recommended shipping the week of 7 December without a condition, while Next steps makes it conditional on the load test passing. I added 'subject to the load test described under Next steps' to the Summary so the two agree. Revert it if you prefer.
The numbers I checked are consistent: 5.80% to 5.98% is a 0.18 point difference and a 3.1% relative lift.

The 'recently viewed' carousel on product pages showed a positive but inconclusive lift in add-to-cart rate on desktop. Add-to-cart rate was 8.1% in control and 8.6% in the variant, a gain of 0.5 percentage points (95% CI -0.04 to +1.04; p = 0.07). The test ran from September 22 to October 20 with about 210,000 sessions per arm, and add-to-cart was our pre-registered primary metric.

Purchases did not show a reliable change. The difference was +0.1 percentage points, and the confidence interval includes zero by a wide margin, so we cannot yet say that the extra add-to-carts are turning into revenue.

Only desktop was tested, so we have no evidence for mobile. Because the primary-metric result is not conclusive and covers desktop only, we are not recommending a rollout to all platforms on this evidence. We would like to agree next steps with the merch team.
items.notes:
A confident tone works here only if it is about what the data shows, so I wrote it as direct statements of the results and the limits. The draft said several things your notes contradict, so I changed them:
- 'Significantly increased' and 'we can be confident the carousel works': the add-to-cart result has p = 0.07 and a CI of -0.04 to +1.04, which includes zero.
- 'Purchases also improved, which confirms...': purchases were +0.1 pp with a CI that crosses zero by a lot.
- 'Clear across the site... ship to all platforms': the test was desktop only.
- 'Pre-registered... adds to our confidence': being the pre-registered primary metric means the add-to-cart result wasn't cherry-picked, but it doesn't make the effect more certain, so I stated it as a fact only.
The rollout recommendation is your call. I replaced the ship-next-sprint line with a conservative one, and you may want to propose a concrete next step, such as extending the test or running mobile.

Since Brightwave Internet launched its AI support assistant, first-contact resolution has risen 4 percentage points, from 62% to 66%. Customer satisfaction moved from 4.21 to 4.26 out of 5, but the difference is not statistically significant, so we do not claim an improvement there.

The revised specification adds length of stay and prior-year admissions as covariates. On the held-out quarter, the area under the ROC curve is 0.78 (95% CI 0.76 to 0.80), compared with 0.74 in the original submission.

Calibration remains acceptable across deciles, although the model under-predicts risk in the highest decile by approximately three percentage points. We recommend that the committee treat the highest-decile estimates with caution until the next recalibration, scheduled for January.

# Store Labor Scheduling Pilot: Findings

## Summary

Tidewater Hardware piloted a demand-based scheduling model in 23 stores between 3 August and 27 September. Understaffed hours fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours in pilot stores, while labor spend stayed within 1% of plan. Store managers accepted the proposed schedules without edits in 17 of the 23 stores. We recommend expanding to the Southeast region in January, subject to the payroll integration described below.

## What we did

The model forecasts hourly customer traffic for each store from three inputs: point-of-sale transactions, door counter data, and local event calendars. It converts the forecast into a staffing requirement using a simple service-level rule, then generates a proposed weekly schedule for the manager to review. Managers could accept the schedule as is or edit it. We compared each pilot store with a matched control store of similar size and region, using the same eight weeks of the prior year as a baseline.

## Results

Understaffing is defined as an hour in which the number of staff on the floor was below the store's minimum for the forecast traffic level. Across the 23 pilot stores, it fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours. In the matched control stores, it moved from 14.0% to 13.1%, so the net improvement attributable to the model is about 3.5 percentage points.

Labor spend in pilot stores was 0.6% above plan, compared with 0.9% above plan in control stores. We do not read much into the difference.

Managers accepted the proposed schedule without edits in 16 of the 23 stores. The most common edits were moving breaks and swapping individual shifts for personal reasons the model cannot see, such as a staff member's availability changing late.

## Limitations

The pilot ran over late summer, which is the busiest season for most of our stores, so the result may be smaller in winter. Two stores in the pilot had a manager change in the middle of the period. Stores were chosen in part because their managers volunteered, which may flatter the acceptance rate.

## Next steps

Payroll integration is the main blocker. Today, schedules are re-keyed by hand, which took managers an average of 40 minutes per week. Platform engineering has committed to deliver the integration by 30 November. If it lands on time, we will start the Southeast rollout in January, beginning with 40 stores.
items.notes:
Please fix one inconsistency before Monday. The Summary says managers accepted schedules without edits in 17 of 23 stores, but the Results section says 16 of 23. I left both as written because I can't tell which is correct.
I also suggest adding the control comparison to the Summary. As written, it gives the raw drop (14.2% to 9.8%). The net improvement against matched controls is about 3.5 points, which is the number the regional leads should anchor on. I left that as your call rather than adding it myself.
The other figures check out: 14.2% to 9.8% against 14.0% to 13.1% in controls gives the net 3.5 points. I made only light wording changes.

The no-show rate rose from 14.9% in Q2 to 17.4% in Q3, an increase of 2.5 percentage points. The rise is concentrated among new patients, whose no-show rate climbed from 15.5% to 21%.

Two changes coincide with the increase. On August 4 we switched SMS reminder vendors, and reminder delivery fell from 97% to about 91% according to the vendor dashboard. The new-patient intake form also became longer in July. We have not yet established whether either change is driving the rise. In particular, we have not yet checked whether the patients who missed appointments are the ones whose reminders were not delivered. We expect that comparison, no-show rates for delivered versus undelivered reminders, next week.
items.notes:
The draft stated conclusions your notes say are not established, so I rewrote that part:
- 'The root cause is the switch to the new SMS provider' and 'Patients who did not receive reminders are the ones missing appointments': your notes mark this as unverified, and the delivered-versus-undelivered comparison hasn't been done.
- 'Fixing the reminder pipeline will bring the rate back to Q2 levels': nothing in the notes supports this prediction.
- 'The longer intake form is irrelevant': it hasn't been tested, and it fits the new-patient concentration at least as well, so I presented it as a second candidate.
Once the delivered-versus-undelivered comparison is done, you'll be able to say much more, and I'm happy to redo this paragraph then.

items.output: ETA model v2 reduces mean absolute error (MAE) from 11.2 to 8.9 minutes, an improvement of about 21%, in an evaluation on five metro areas (Austin, Denver, Columbus, Tampa, and Phoenix) using August 1-31 data. V2 adds a live-traffic feature to the v1 inputs. Two areas are not yet covered. Rural routes, where v1 was already weaker, have not been evaluated. We are targeting a ship to the five metros on December 1; a wider rollout depends on a rural evaluation in Q1. Next steps are to document the evaluation and plan the rollout.

- 'Across our entire delivery network': the evaluation covered five metros only.

Thanks for the opportunity to dig into the onboarding funnel data. Here are the key takeaways.

Based on our analysis, a substantial portion of new sign-ups appear to drop off at the identity verification step. About 40% of users who start verification never complete it. This may be linked to the document upload requirement, but we have not isolated the cause.

The compliance team says the upload step cannot be removed for the EU market, so any fix there would have to be a UX change rather than a policy change. The design team believes a redesigned upload screen could recover a meaningful share of these users, but this is a hypothesis, not a measured result.

We plan to run a prototype test in the week of 8 February and will circulate results by the end of that month. Please reach out with any thoughts or questions.
items.notes: What was making it sound off: the opener ('truly eye-opening experience') and the 'high-level overview' framing are more enthusiasm than a PM wants from a findings note. 'Could potentially' stacked two hedges. The closer was generic. The content itself (the 40% figure, the unisolated cause, the EU compliance constraint, the hypothesis label and the February timeline) is solid, so I kept all of it and just made it more direct and split it into short paragraphs.
